# Federal Requirements and Deposition {#sec-federal}

The Data Management and Sharing Plan (DMSP) was written with the
grant application, two years before the first dataset existed,
and NIH program staff approved it as a term of the award. The
plan written in the last hour before submission said 'data will
be deposited in a public repository at publication', and nobody
objected. At publication the analyst discovers what the sentence
committed to: the participant-level data carry protected health
information (PHI), the repository named accepts only
de-identified data, and unconditional public release was never
something the consent form allowed. Nothing failed when the plan
was written; it fails at the moment it is executed. Writing the
plan so that it can be carried out is the subject of
@sec-federal-dmsp, beside the statistical analysis plan. This
chapter is about the end of the project: what the federal
public-access policies require at publication, which repository
each artifact goes to, and the check that runs before anything
leaves the institution.

## What the policies require {#sec-federal-policy}

The DMSP (@sec-federal-dmsp) said what the project would share,
where, and when; this section and the next are the end of the
project, when that plan is carried out.

The policy direction in the United States has been toward public
access for publicly funded research: shorter embargoes, a wider
scope (data and code, not only papers), and more auditing. The
details change faster than any book, so they live in one dated
table, @tbl-federal-asof, and the prose keeps to what has been
stable.

| Agency | Requirement | Effective | Source | Verified |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| OSTP, for all funding agencies | Peer-reviewed publications and their supporting data freely available at publication, without embargo; persistent identifiers | Memo issued 2022-08-25; agency policies in effect by 2025-12-31 | @usshi2022ostp | 2026-10-09[^asof-ostp] |
| NIH | DMSP with every application that will generate scientific data; approved plan is a term of award | Applications for receipt dates on or after 2023-01-25 | NOT-OD-21-013 | 2026-10-09 |
| NIH | 2024 Public Access Policy: accepted manuscript submitted to PubMed Central on acceptance, public on the official publication date, no embargo | Manuscripts accepted on or after 2025-07-01 | NIH public access policy page | 2026-10-09 |
| NIH | Clinical trials registered and results reported on ClinicalTrials.gov | 2017 | NIH policy on dissemination of clinical trial information | |
| NSF | Data Management Plan of up to two pages with each proposal | | NSF proposal guide | |
| DOE, CDC, NASA | Agency public-access plans under the OSTP memo | | Agency pages | |
| FDA | CDISC-standard data for regulatory submissions (@sec-cdisc) | | FDA study data standards | |

: Federal requirements as of 2026-10-09. A blank 'Verified' cell
means the author has not checked that entry against its source;
check it before relying on it, and record the date you did.
{#tbl-federal-asof}

[^asof-ostp]: Checked against secondary sources. Trade-press
    reports in 2026 that OSTP may reconsider the zero-embargo
    requirement were unconfirmed as of that date.

Three implications have held through every revision, and they
are the ones that change what you do:

- **Plan for the publication to be open from day one.** No
  embargo affects journal selection, and the accepted manuscript,
  not only the typeset article, is what NIH requires.
- **Plan for the data to be deposited and citable at
  publication.** This affects the timeline: de-identification and
  repository review take weeks.
- **Plan for the code to be deposited too.** Funders increasingly
  expect it even where it is not explicitly required, and a
  results claim without the code that produced it cannot be
  checked.

For a project funded by more than one agency, the most
restrictive policy applies. The Food and Drug Administration
(FDA) regime for industry trials is different in kind: it is a
submission standard rather than an open-data policy, more
structured, and serves the same reproducibility role inside the
regulatory process (@sec-cdisc).

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**A policy summary copied from a colleague's plan is already out
of date.** Effective dates, notice numbers, and repository lists
change, and a plan that cites the superseded policy reads as
current to everyone who does not check. Cite the dated source,
and re-verify each row of a table like @tbl-federal-asof before
you submit.
:::

### Exercises

1. Two HF-HOME papers are funded by NIH. Paper A was accepted on
   2025-06-20 and Paper B on 2025-07-10, and both are published
   in September 2025. Under the 2024 NIH Public Access Policy,
   which must be public in PubMed Central on its publication
   date?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
Paper B. The 2024 policy applies to manuscripts *accepted* on or
after 2025-07-01, so the acceptance date, not the publication
date, decides. Paper A falls under the earlier policy, which
allowed an embargo of up to 12 months. A plan that keys on the
publication date gets this wrong for every paper in the pipeline
on the changeover date.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Why does this chapter keep policy dates in one
table rather than in the prose where each is discussed?

**Answer.** Because they are perishable facts, and a date in a
sentence is never re-checked, while a table with a 'Verified'
column shows its own age. The prose keeps what has been stable
(open at publication, data citable at publication, code
deposited), which is what changes your plan; the table carries
what changes from year to year.
:::

## Choosing a repository {#sec-federal-repository}

The choice is less open than the list of candidates suggests,
because the data type and the access restriction between them
determine it. @fig-repo-choice is the decision as it actually
runs.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-repo-choice
%%| fig-alt: "Decision flowchart for choosing a deposition target.
%%|   The first question asks whether the artifact contains
%%|   participant-level or restricted data. If yes, the data are
%%|   de-identified first, then deposited under controlled access
%%|   in a domain repository such as dbGaP, TCIA, BioLINCC, Vivli or
%%|   ICPSR where one fits, otherwise in institutional controlled
%%|   access plus a synthetic public surrogate. If no, a
%%|   second question separates code from data: code goes to GitHub
%%|   with a Zenodo release for the DOI, while data goes to a domain
%%|   repository such as GEO, SRA, NeuroVault or ICPSR where one
%%|   exists, otherwise Zenodo, OSF or Dryad."
%%| fig-cap: "Choosing a deposition target. The first question is
%%|   whether the artifact carries participant-level or restricted
%%|   data, which are de-identified before any deposit; the second
%%|   is whether a repository specific to the data type exists. A
%%|   general-purpose repository is the right answer for code and
%%|   supplementary tables and the wrong answer for primary
%%|   genomic or imaging data."
flowchart TD
  A{"Participant-level<br/>or restricted data?"}
  A -->|"Yes"| X["De-identify first<br/><i>before any deposit</i>"]
  X --> B{"Domain repository<br/>for this data type?"}
  A -->|"No"| C{"Code, or data?"}
  B -->|"Yes"| D["dbGaP, TCIA, BioLINCC,<br/>Vivli, ICPSR<br/><i>controlled access, DUA</i>"]
  B -->|"No"| E["Institutional controlled<br/>access, plus a synthetic<br/>public surrogate"]
  C -->|"Code"| F["GitHub for work,<br/>Zenodo release for the DOI"]
  C -->|"Data"| G{"Domain repository<br/>for this data type?"}
  G -->|"Yes"| H["GEO, SRA, NeuroVault,<br/>ICPSR"]
  G -->|"No"| I["Zenodo, OSF, or Dryad"]
```

### Matching the artifact to a repository

Each domain repository has a defined scope, and naming one
outside it is the commonest error in a draft plan.
@tbl-federal-repo-match pairs the artifacts a clinical project
produces with a repository and an access mode. For every
repository named, the default is de-identified data; deposit more
only where the repository's terms and your governing agreements
explicitly allow it.

| Artifact | PHI as collected? | Appropriate repository | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Clinical-trial participant data | Yes; de-identify first | BioLINCC (NHLBI studies), Vivli, or an archive the funding institute designates | Controlled, DUA |
| Genotype paired with phenotype | Yes; de-identify first | dbGaP | Controlled |
| Cancer imaging | Yes; de-identify first (headers, burned-in text, faces) | The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA) | Open or controlled |
| Gene-expression or sequencing data | Usually not, for non-human studies | GEO, SRA | Open |
| Social-science and observational survey data | Often; de-identify first | ICPSR | Open or controlled |
| Code, data dictionary, summary tables | No | GitHub, archived to Zenodo | Open |
| Synthetic surrogate dataset | No | Zenodo or OSF | Open |

: Matching the artifact to the repository. dbGaP and TCIA have
narrow scopes; clinical data in general belong in neither.
{#tbl-federal-repo-match}

### Hosting is not archiving

For deposition, a repository must provide a persistent
identifier, a preservation commitment, open or controlled access
as needed, and metadata fields for the discipline.
@tbl-federal-hosting compares the three kinds a biostatistician
uses.

| | GitHub | Zenodo, OSF, Dryad | Domain repository |
|---|---|---|---|
| Persistent identifier | No; URLs change | DOI per version | Accession number or DOI |
| Preservation commitment | None | Yes, stated by the repository | Yes |
| Fixed version | No; `main` moves | Snapshot at deposit | Snapshot at deposit |
| Access control | Public or private only | Mostly open | Controlled access with DUA |
| Best for | Working code | Code releases, supplementary data | Primary participant-level, genomic, imaging data |

: Hosting, general-purpose archiving, and domain archiving.
Dryad curates and charges a fee; OSF supports preregistration;
Zenodo deposits a GitHub release automatically.
{#tbl-federal-hosting}

The practical pattern is therefore to work in GitHub and archive
to Zenodo at each tagged release, and to deposit primary data in
the domain repository when one exists. Institutional repositories
vary in quality; they are an acceptable backup and not always
sufficient as the primary deposit.

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
> **Context.** A two-arm clinical trial funded by NIH. Artifacts:
> de-identified participant-level CRF and outcome data, a
> codebook, analysis code, summary tables, and a synthetic
> surrogate dataset. The funding institute is named in the
> attachment. No data rows.
>
> **Constraints.** For each artifact, propose a repository and an
> access mode, and quote the repository's own statement of scope
> that admits this data type. Assume every participant-level
> artifact is de-identified and none is PHI.
>
> **Criteria.** No repository is proposed outside its stated
> scope; participant-level data are under controlled access; a
> general-purpose repository is proposed only for code, tables,
> or synthetic data.

*Failure mode.* The model reaches for dbGaP or TCIA for clinical
data that fit neither (dbGaP is for studies pairing genotype with
phenotype, TCIA for cancer imaging), or defaults to Zenodo for
participant-level data because it is 'general-purpose'. *Check.*
Compare each proposal with @tbl-federal-repo-match, read the
repository's scope statement yourself, and see which repositories
the leading trials in your field cite.
:::

### Exercises

2. Name an appropriate repository and access mode for each:
   (a) RNA-seq counts from a mouse experiment; (b) HF-HOME's
   participant-level outcome data; (c) the analysis code and
   codebook for (b); (d) a synthetic dataset that lets a reviewer
   run the code for (b).

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
(a) GEO for the counts (and SRA for raw reads), open access; no
PHI is involved. (b) A clinical-trial repository under controlled
access with a DUA (BioLINCC if NHLBI funds the trial and requests
the data, otherwise Vivli or the institute's designated archive),
and only after de-identification; never dbGaP, which is for
genotype-phenotype studies. (c) GitHub for working, archived to
Zenodo at a tagged release for the DOI, open. (d) Zenodo or OSF,
open, with the generator code if possible, so that the reviewer
can see how the surrogate was made.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Your code is public on GitHub, with a README, a
license, and a full commit history. The DMSP asks where the code
will be preserved. Is a GitHub URL an adequate answer?

**Answer.** No, and not because GitHub is unreliable: it makes no
preservation commitment. A repository can be deleted, renamed,
made private, or removed when an account lapses, and the citation
then points at nothing. A repository also has no fixed identity;
`main` today is not `main` next year, so a bare URL does not say
which version produced the results. A Zenodo release mints a DOI
that resolves permanently and snapshots the repository at that
commit, which is why the pattern pairs them. The same distinction
applies to the SAP tag of @sec-analysis-plan: a tag organizes; an
external, timestamped, immutable record is what makes it evidence.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 5: pre-specify, then tag.** The DMSP was the
   pre-specification of sharing; check the deposit against each
   of its elements, and build deposition into the pipeline.
2. **Habit 4: pin the environment.** The plan points to
   `renv.lock` and a Dockerfile, and the deposit contains them.
3. **Habit 1: the compendium is the unit.** Deposit code, data,
   environment, and document together, each in the repository
   whose scope fits it, with de-identified data under controlled
   access.

## Cumulative practice

3. *Cumulative (uses @sec-federal-dmsp and @sec-renv).* Rebuild
   `manifest` from the Verification in @sec-federal-dmsp, and
   extend it into a deposit manifest: add
   a `destination` column (controlled-access repository or
   Zenodo), add the codebook, `renv.lock`, and the Dockerfile as
   rows, and write a `stopifnot()` that fails if anything bound
   for an open repository is participant-level or has identifier
   columns.
4. *On your own work (no key).* Pick a recent biomedical paper in
   your field. Check whether its data and code are reachable at a
   persistent identifier, whether the access mode suits the data,
   and whether the paper's data-availability statement could be
   checked by a reader. Write one paragraph classifying its
   compliance.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution to exercise 3'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-25c-3
#| message: false
library(dplyr)

hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")
identifiers <- c("mrn", "first_name", "last_name", "dob", "zip",
                 "phone", "discharge_date", "rand_date",
                 "visit_date", "event_date", "readmit_date",
                 "death_date")
files <- list.files(hf_dir, pattern = "\\.csv$")
manifest <- tibble(
  file = files,
  identifier_columns = vapply(files, \(f) {
    cols <- names(readr::read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, f), n_max = 0,
                                  show_col_types = FALSE))
    paste(intersect(cols, identifiers), collapse = ", ")
  }, character(1))
)

deposit <- manifest |>
  mutate(participant_level = TRUE,
         destination = "Controlled access, de-identified release") |>
  bind_rows(tibble(
    file = c("README.md (codebook)", "renv.lock", "Dockerfile"),
    identifier_columns = "",
    participant_level = FALSE,
    destination = "Zenodo (open)"
  ))

open_files <- deposit |> filter(destination == "Zenodo (open)")
stopifnot(!any(open_files$participant_level),
          all(open_files$identifier_columns == ""))
deposit |> select(file, participant_level, destination)
```

The two conditions encode two different rules, and the first is
the one people forget. `labs.csv` and `medications.csv` carry no
identifier column, so a check on identifier columns alone would
let them go to Zenodo; they are still participant-level records,
linked by `patient_id` to every other file, and belong under
controlled access with the de-identified release. Even then the
assertion is a structural check: it confirms that a listed
identifier is absent, not that the data are safe to publish
(@sec-deident-risk).
:::

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Do | Guards against |
|---|---|---|
| Carry out the DMSP | Check the deposit against each element (@sec-federal-dmsp) | A plan approved and never executed |
| Plan data sharing | De-identified data under controlled access; synthetic or summary data open | PHI or participant-level data in an open repository |
| Describe the environment | Point to `renv.lock` and a Dockerfile (@sec-renv) | 'Standard R packages' |
| Track policy | One dated table with a 'Verified' column | Superseded requirements cited as current |
| Archive code | GitHub release archived to Zenodo for a DOI | A citation to a URL that moves |
| Choose a repository | Match the data type to the repository's stated scope | dbGaP or TCIA for general clinical data |
| Check before deposit | Manifest of files and identifier columns, with an assertion | An identifier leaving in a file nobody opened |

: Federal requirements and deposition at a glance.
{#tbl-federal-cheat-sheet}

## Further reading

- [@usshi2022ostp], the 2022 OSTP 'Nelson memo'.
- The NIH data management and sharing policy pages at
  `grants.nih.gov`, the authoritative source for the DMSP and the
  2024 Public Access Policy.
- ICPSR's *Guide to Social Science Data Preparation and
  Archiving*, portable to biostatistics for metadata practice.

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-25c}

1. The Nelson memo (August 2022) directs federal agencies that
   fund research to make peer-reviewed publications, and the
   scientific data underlying them, freely available at
   publication, without the 12-month embargo that the 2013
   Holdren memo allowed, and with persistent identifiers. Agencies
   were to have their updated policies in effect by the end of
   2025; @tbl-federal-asof records each agency's implementation
   and when it was last checked.
2. Each has a narrow scope. dbGaP is for studies that pair
   genotype with phenotype, and TCIA for cancer imaging; general
   clinical-trial data fit neither, and belong, de-identified and
   under controlled access, in a clinical-trial repository such as
   BioLINCC or Vivli (@tbl-federal-repo-match).
3. No. GitHub hosts; it makes no preservation commitment, and a
   URL names no fixed version. Archive a tagged release to Zenodo
   (or a domain repository) for a DOI and a snapshot, and cite
   that.
